description: Recorded from the audience on DAT at 19 Broadway in Fairfax on August 23, 1999. The two reels are mislabeled, so it isn’t certain which is truly Part 1 and which is Part 2 — but one is clean and the other heavily distorted, and the archive keeps them separate here rather than guess.

The main 14-song set comes from the clean tape. Mostly originals, including an early version of “Rugburns” before it found its familiar shape, alongside covers of Steve Poltz’s “Single Life,” Bruce Springsteen’s “Highway Patrolman,” Lefty Frizzell’s “Long Black Veil,” and Paddy Nash’s “Model Family Man.”

A second batch of 7 songs was later recovered from the distorted reel and is kept separate below, labeled “Part 1 (Distorted)” — rough listening in places, but archived rather than lost. It includes an alternate version of “ABC,” another early take of “Rugburns,” and three songs that don’t appear anywhere else in the archive: “Troy,” “The Kiss,” and “Da Da Da (Slave to an Angel).”
Straightforward hand-edits and the usual loudness normalization to the archive standard throughout; no noise reduction or EQ needed on either tape.

Twenty-nine of the thirty-four tracks needed help beyond plain linear gain: five are handled by the applause-only limiter and sixteen qualify for the sparse-transient-cap mode, reaching the full −20 LUFS target instead of landing quieter. Reprocessed this Mad Hannans set at Cafe Java again, this time under a new workflow (v8) built for tapes where the mic sat close to the drums: a millisecond-scale true-peak limiter now catches only the sharpest instant of an isolated musical transient — a snare hit, a strum — while the surrounding performance keeps its full, untouched gain, letting more tracks reach the archive's −20 LUFS standard instead of landing several dB quieter. Fifteen of the twenty-two tracks qualified and are now capped this way; “Rocky Road to Dublin / Star of County Down” needed more recovery than the policy's 6 dB ceiling allows, so it lands at −21.6 LUFS instead of −20 — inaudibly quieter, never over-shaved. “Truck” and “Anna May” are untouched by this change: both were already correctly handled by an earlier, unrelated fix that limits only audience applause at a track's edges, not the music.
